content: Calcium channel blockers should not be used in the treatment of non-severe hypertension during pregnancy due to safety concerns. Clinical trials have evaluated various oral beta-blockers, including acebutolol, atenolol, labetalol, mepindolol, metoprolol, oxprenolol, pindolol, and propranolol, at different dosages. However, the optimal beta-blocker choice and dosing regimen for this indication remain undetermined. Atenolol and metoprolol are included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and are widely accessible in many countries. The use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and sodium nitroprusside is contraindicated during pregnancy due to safety concerns. In 2015, approximately 295,000 women and adolescent girls died from pregnancy and childbirth-related complications, with 99% of these deaths occurring in low-resource settings. Hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, and sepsis account for over half of all maternal deaths globally. Improving maternal healthcare quality is essential to achieving the health targets of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). International human rights laws and treaties obligate states to ensure that women and adolescent girls can exercise their right to health and life preservation during pregnancy and childbirth. This is integral to their sexual and reproductive health rights and living a life of dignity. The WHO envisions a world where every pregnant woman and newborn receives quality care throughout pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period. Evidence suggests that effective interventions exist at reasonable costs to prevent or treat nearly all life-threatening maternal complications. Optimal adaptation and implementation of existing research findings could alleviate nearly two-thirds of the global maternal and neonatal disease burden. Healthcare providers at all levels, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), require access to appropriate medications and training in relevant procedures to deliver quality maternal healthcare. Policymakers, healthcare managers, and other stakeholders also need up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations to inform clinical policies and practices, optimize care quality, and improve healthcare outcomes. Hypertensive disorders during pregnancy are a significant cause of severe morbidity, long-term disability, and maternal and neonatal mortality, accounting for approximately 14% of all maternal deaths worldwide. In 2011, the WHO issued 22 recommendations for preventing and treating pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, developed using rigorous guideline development standards, including evidence synthesis, the GRADE methodology, and input from an international panel of experts. These recommendations included two on antihypertensive drugs for severe hypertension during pregnancy. At that time, the guideline development group reviewed evidence on antihypertensive drugs for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy but decided not to issue a recommendation. The recommendations for severe hypertension were updated in 2018. Hypertension during pregnancy is common, affecting approximately one in ten pregnancies. It is a progressive condition that can lead to severe acute morbidity, long-term disability, and death. Prevention, early diagnosis, and timely, appropriate treatment to lower blood pressure in pregnant women with hypertension are critical management strategies. Emerging evidence suggests that antihypertensive treatment in women with non-severe hypertension during pregnancy may prevent progression to more severe disease. In response to this new evidence, the WHO prioritized developing recommendations on antihypertensive drug treatment for non-severe hypertension during pregnancy. The primary goal of these recommendations is to improve care quality and outcomes for pregnant women, particularly concerning hypertensive disorders. These recommendations aim to support the sustainable implementation of drug treatment for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy globally. The target audience for these recommendations includes those responsible for developing national and local health guidelines and protocols, particularly those related to hypertensive disorders in pregnancy. This includes midwives, nurses, general medical practitioners, obstetricians, maternal and child health program managers, and relevant staff in health ministries. The recommendations are also relevant to professional societies, non-governmental organizations promoting people-centered maternal care, and implementers of maternal and child health programs. The recommendations aim to enhance countries' capacity to address non-severe hypertension during pregnancy and prioritize essential actions in national health policies, strategies, and plans. For women with non-severe (mild to moderate) hypertension during pregnancy, the recommendations explore whether treatment with any antihypertensive drug, a specific class of antihypertensive drugs, or one antihypertensive drug compared to another improves maternal and perinatal outcomes. The affected population includes pregnant women in low-, middle-, or high-income settings, particularly those with non-severe hypertension during pregnancy. The recommendations were developed using standardized procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. This process included identifying priority questions and critical outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, impact evaluation, and updating. The WHO identified the use of antihypertensive drugs for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy as a high priority for developing recommendations in response to new evidence. Six main groups contributed to this process, including the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG), WHO Steering Group, Guideline Development Group (GDG), External Review Group, Evidence Synthesis Group, and external partners and observers. The Executive GSG, an independent panel of 14 external experts and stakeholders from six WHO regions, advised on prioritizing maternal and perinatal health questions for recommendation development or updating. The WHO Steering Group, comprising staff from the Departments of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research (SRH) and Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health and Ageing (MCA), managed the guideline development process. They drafted key recommendation questions, identified systematic review teams and guideline methodologists, and supervised evidence synthesis and retrieval. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included 17 external experts and stakeholders with expertise in research, guideline development methods, and clinical policy and programs related to maternal and perinatal health. They appraised and interpreted evidence to formulate recommendations and reviewed and approved the final guideline document. The External Review Group, consisting of eight technical experts, reviewed the final document for factual accuracy, language clarity, contextual issues, and implications. They ensured that decision-making processes incorporated contextual values and user preferences without altering the GDG's recommendations. The Evidence Synthesis Group conducted a systematic review, supported by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group, to evaluate the effects of antihypertensive drugs for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy. The review followed Cochrane's standard procedures and served as the primary evidence source for the recommendations. External partners and observers, including representatives from organizations like USAID, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics, participated in the GDG meeting as observers. These organizations have a history of collaboration with WHO in guideline dissemination and implementation. The critical outcomes for these recommendations align with those from the 2011 WHO recommendations on pre-eclampsia and eclampsia prevention and treatment. These outcomes were identified through systematic reviews and prioritized by the 2011 GDG panel. All outcomes were included in the scope of this document for evidence searching, retrieval, grading, and recommendation formulation. Evidence on the effects of antihypertensive drugs for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy was synthesized and appraised using the GRADE methodology.
